title: Ephemeral threshold surge hypotheses and sleuthing notebook
content:
TL;DR:
We saw a ~90m window of p99/p995 latency climb and streaming fragmentation affecting hosted-api streaming sessions. Immediate surface cause: an ephemeral concurrency threshold (autoscaler cooldown + new batching policy) pushed a small set of edge acceptors into a tight retry loop; that loop amplified KV-cache rehydration pressure on a few model shards which then backpressured the multiplexer, cascading into increased queuing and session fragmentation.

Impact summary:
- Start: 2029-03-15T02:12:45Z — end: 2029-03-15T03:45:12Z (mitigated, full recovery by 03:50Z)
- Affected: ~1.8% of customers (topologically concentrated in EU-West region), primarily streaming endpoints and long-token completion flows.
- Symptoms: TTFB spikes, repeated stream reattachments, higher 5xx for streaming writes, transient token loss on edge reconnects.

What made this tricky / why it wasn't a simple autoscale bug:
- The autoscaler did *something expected* (scale down due to ephemeral utilization dip) but the new batching policy introduced a small change in acceptor behavior: acceptors started holding onto partial batches longer before flushing, which increased per-acceptor KV cache pressure briefly. That combined with a heartbeat oscillation (roughly 20–30s) between acceptor health checks and the edge keepalive resulted in multiple acceptors being marked degraded at once.
- Degraded acceptor set => client rejections and retries concentrated on remaining acceptors => their KV cache hit rate collapsed and rehydration throughput spiked.

Investigation timeline (notes from on-call):
- 02:12:30Z — Pager triggered: streaming p99 > 8s for 3 consecutive 1m windows (alert SRE-4238-trigger-1).
- 02:13:10Z — grabbed top of thread, collected: edge acceptor counts, autoscaler events, model-shard KV eviction rates, streaming write 5xx rates.
- 02:14:02Z — hypothesis 1 (autoscale flapping) created; temporarily bumped reserved headroom on EU-W nodes (manual pool +2 acceptors) — immediate partial improvement in p95 but p99 still high.
- 02:18:21Z — observed correlated spikes in kv-cache miss metric and acceptor eviction counter for shards serving gpt-small-enc variants.
- 02:25:44Z — hypothesis 2 (kv-cache bulk rehydration due to request fan-in) created; rolled a targeted fallback to a compatible quantized model on the worst-hit tenant prefix — latency improved for that tenant.
- 02:40:03Z — noted heartbeat/keepalive timing skew in EU-W edge fleet after edge proxy update (PR #2051) — added to longlist.
- 03:10:00Z — implemented short-term mitigation: revert batching policy change on a canary subset of acceptors + increase KV cache prefetch throttle.
- 03:31:10Z — telemetry showed queueing and rehydration pressure dropping; by 03:45Z most metrics returned to baseline.

Observations and raw signals we pulled:
- grafana query: topk(10, rate(stream_write_5xx_total[1m])) showed EUW hosts spike 02:12–02:45.
- internal log sample: "acceptor: partial_batch_timeout exceeded, holding batch for 27ms" (new batching policy set to 25ms) — previously 10ms.
- kv cache metric: kv_rehydrate_ops/sec jumped 12x on shard-3 which holds several high-traffic prefixes.
- autoscaler audit: scaleDownEvents at 02:11:20Z for acceptor group C (eu-west) with cooldown window still active from prior scaleUp at 01:55Z.
- edge proxy changelog: proxy v3.14.2 rolled 02:09–02:10 with adjusted keepalive jitter (originally intended to reduce churn).

Hypotheses we tested (and how):
1) Autoscaler thrash / cooldown mismatch => tested by temporarily pinning headroom and watching whether p99 improves. Result: partial — p95 improved but p99 not fully resolved. Suggests autoscale contributed but wasn't sole cause.
2) Batching policy change increased partial-batch hold-time causing KV cache hot-spotting => tested by reverting policy on a canary subset. Result: clear reduction in kv_rehydrate_ops and p99 decreased ~40%.
3) Edge keepalive/heartbeat oscillation caused synchronous client reconnect bursts => tested by inspecting edge keepalive timing distributions and correlating with acceptor health markers and reconnect counts. Result: strong correlation; jitter removal in new proxy left keepalives more synchronous leading to small but synchronized reconnect floods.
4) Client-side retry amplification (SDK change) => low probability; scanned SDK release notes and client-metrics; no evidence.

Root cause (conclusion):
A confluence of three small changes produced emergent behavior: (A) batching policy increased batch wait to 25ms (was 10ms) which subtly changed acceptor timing, (B) proxy keepalive jitter reduction made reconnects more synchronized across clients, and (C) autoscaler cooldown combined with a previous scaleUp left the EUW acceptor group with reduced headroom. Together these produced concentrated request fan-in to a few acceptors which caused shard-local KV cache rehydration spikes that backpressured multiplexers and manifested as high p99 streaming latency and fragmentation.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- 02:22–02:35Z: Manually increased reserved headroom for eu-west acceptor pool (+2 acceptors) to give breathing room.
- 03:10Z: Reverted batching policy change on canary acceptors (rollback PR 2146 canary -> full rollback if stability holds).
- 03:12Z: Applied a temporary KV-cache prefetch throttle (limit rehydrate concurrency from 16 -> 4) on shard-3 and shard-5.
- 03:20Z: Rolled back edge proxy jitter change to previous setting on a subset of nodes while monitoring reconnect distribution.

Why those mitigations worked:
- Extra headroom spread load immediately, reducing instantaneous fan-in.
- Rolling back batching reduced partial-batch hold time, which lowered simultaneous cache pressure.
- Throttling rehydration prevented cache backpressure from starving multiplexer threads.

Permanent fixes & follow-ups (owners and tickets):
- ACTION SRE-4238-1 owner: Carlos Rivera — implement autoscaler cooldown safety net to forbid scale-down if batchPolicy.change_at < 15m (ticket SRE-4260).
- ACTION SRE-4238-2 owner: Elena Patel — revert batching policy change and add invariant tests that quantify kv-rehydrate ops under synthetic fan-in (ticket INF-3181).
- ACTION SRE-4238-3 owner: Platform Eng — rework edge keepalive jitter configuration to avoid synchronous reconnect windows; add chaos test to simulate jitter loss (ticket EDGE-594).
- ACTION SRE-4238-4 owner: Runtime Team — add kv-cache admission controller that caps rehydrate concurrency per shard and exposes a 'pressure' metric (ticket RUNTIME-1129).
- ACTION SRE-4238-5 owner: Maya Chen — update hosted-api streaming runbook: add step for "detect simultaneous acceptor degrade -> increase headroom" and include a dashboard panel that overlays acceptor_count, kv_rehydrate_ops, and stream_reconnect_rate (ticket RUNBOOK-77).

Runbook / playbook changes to author now (notes to self):
- Add quick triage checklist: 1) check acceptor headroom trend & autoscaler events; 2) overlay kv cache misses and top shards; 3) inspect recent batching/acceptor config rollouts; 4) check edge keepalive jitter config; 5) apply emergency headroom if >1 acceptor degrades in <60s.
- Add quick query snippets to runbook (copy-paste friendly):
  - grafana: topk(5, sum(rate(kv_rehydrate_ops[1m])) by (shard))
  - logql: {component="acceptor"} |= "partial_batch_timeout" | json | line_format "{{.host}} {{.timeout_ms}}"
  - metrics: sum by(region) (acceptor_healthy_count) ; compare to autoscaler events log
- Triage play: prefer reverting batching change on canary acceptors before touching global autoscaler configs. Revert steps and PR numbers in runbook.

Post-incident retrospective observations (soft lessons):
- Small timing changes in multiple subsystems can couple nonlinearly — our tests focused on unit behaviors but not on cross-layer timing interactions. Need a harness for multi-subsystem timing perturbation testing.
- Autoscaler safety nets need to be conservative when other policies modify request pacing (batching, acceptor waits).
- Edge changes that reduce jitter can be harmful at scale — measured jitter is useful as a resilience knob, not just noise.

Appendix: useful queries / commands run during incident (for future reuse):
- kubectl get events -n hosted-api | grep autoscaler | tail -n 50
- curl "https://internal-grafana/api/datasources/proxy/1/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(kv_rehydrate_ops[1m])) by (shard)" | jq .
- jq filter used on logs: jq '. | {ts, host, msg, shard, prefix}' < acceptor-logs.jsonl | grep partial_batch_timeout | head -n 40

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Why did shard-3 have such low effective cache hit rate compared to neighboring shards given similar traffic profiles? (follow-up: examine placement, memory fragmentation, and shard pinning behavior).
- Is there a better long-term approach than throttling rehydrate concurrency (e.g., background prefetch / predictive KV warming)?

Notes to on-call/reader: this doc is a working notebook, not the final postmortem. When we lock actions into tickets, update this doc pointer from draft -> final and add metric diffs showing before/after improvements.

Slack thread references: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C0SRE/p1591234000000200
SRE-4238 incident page (w/ raw traces): s3://redwood-incident-archives/sre-4238/

End of notes.
